what_it_does: Engineers designing custom AI accelerator chips often write their hardware descriptions in high-level C/C++ code and use a tool called High-Level Synthesis (HLS) to automatically translate that into a chip blueprint — but testing whether the design actually behaves correctly and how long it will take to run requires either a fast-but-wrong software simulation or an accurate-but-agonizingly-slow hardware-level simulation (taking hours to days). OmniSim is a new simulator that achieves near-C-code speed while matching the cycle-accurate correctness of hardware simulation, and crucially it is the first tool to correctly handle complex hardware designs involving feedback loops and non-blocking data channels that all existing commercial and academic tools explicitly refuse to simulate.
method_in_detail:
The problem. HLS designs describe hardware where multiple modules run truly simultaneously, communicating through FIFO queues (first-in-first-out buffers — like a conveyor belt between workers). There are two tricky variants: non-blocking reads/writes (the module checks if data is available but doesn't wait — it just records "nothing there" and moves on), and cyclic dependencies (module A waits for data from module B, but B also waits for data from A). Standard software multi-threading assigns modules to OS threads, but the operating system's scheduler decides who runs when — a completely different order than real hardware. This makes timers, congestion-aware routers, and feedback controllers give wrong answers under software simulation.

The idea. OmniSim separates simulation into two interleaved threads: many Functionality Simulation (Func Sim) threads — one per hardware module — that execute the C code and record events, and one dedicated Performance Simulation (Perf Sim) thread that maintains a precise table of when each FIFO read or write occurs in hardware clock cycles.

How it works. Func Sim threads run freely and fast, building up a partial dependency graph (recording that "write W must complete before read R"). Whenever a Func Sim thread hits a non-blocking FIFO access, it cannot proceed without knowing the exact hardware cycle — because the design's behavior branches depending on whether the FIFO was full or empty at that precise moment. The thread pauses and posts a query to a shared pool. When all Func Sim threads are paused, the Perf Sim thread consults its FIFO timing table, compares hardware-cycle timestamps (not OS-thread scheduling order), resolves as many queries as possible, and resumes the threads. This accurately reproduces the hardware's real behavior regardless of how the OS happens to schedule the software threads.

The key design choice. Func Sim and Perf Sim threads overlap their execution — the Perf Sim thread processes incoming events while Func Sim threads are still generating them, rather than running two fully separate phases. This overlap is both essential for correctness on complex designs and also faster than the previous best tool (LightningSim) on simpler designs.

The result. OmniSim correctly simulates eleven designs that all existing HLS tools fail on, with cycle counts within 0.09% of gold-standard hardware co-simulation, and runs 30.7× faster than that co-simulation. On the previous simulator's own benchmark suite, OmniSim achieves up to 6.61× speedup.
